instructor: No weak points. He made complex topics intelligible for us. He provided historical background so I could see how these philosophers were interconnected (not just similarities or continuing the same argument but also how they objected each other). We highly engaged with primary sources and also the secondary literature about them. I think it is the Alireza Hoca's strongest point in both Rationalists and Empiricists course, we learned how to get into secondary literature without over/underestimating the primary sources. He contributed with his own opinions/objections both when discussing the primary sources and the secondary literature. He respects students and is easy to reach. Even when someone called p->q, q therefore p modus ponens (I was shocked), I didn't saw any negative feeling in his face. He is willing to help anyone. My respect for him was heightened when right after he explained how memory and imagination differ in Hume's philosophy, someone asked what is the difference between them and he answered them calmly and with patience. His points on Newton's influence were amazing. I feel incredibly lucky to have taken Rationalists and Empiricists from him.

He is the kindest teacher I have ever met. He always tries to act in the best interest of his students. I really appreciate his teaching style. Sometimes, even though the subject matter is not particularly engaging, he manages to make it enjoyable.

He’s very good at sparking interest in his classes. I took his course as a restricted elective during my final semester, and even though I’d never been interested in philosophy before, I learned a lot without even realizing it, thanks to Professor Ali. He’s open to all kinds of viewpoints and arguments, and he listens to everyone and every idea with respect, never interrupting and always with understanding. His grading is very fair. If you truly do everything required in the course and attend classes regularly, you’ll learn a great deal in this class. Professor Ali’s dedication and enthusiasm for the course rub off on you, and even the most disinterested student might find themselves listening to the lecture and taking notes. If you need to take a restricted elective, you definitely shouldn’t miss this course.

instructor: The lecture was good and intellectually challenging, which is a good thing. The only bad part of the lecture is that it may sometimes be too challenging. It is hard to keep the balance at this point, and Fatollahi did a good job overall. Discussions in the class were good. The professor gave each student enough space/time to talk, encouraging students to talk, which was good because I was kind of shy at the beginning of the class due to I did not know much about the stuff. He was serious; the material and content of the class were good/intriguing. The approach of the professor was kind of inspiring.
The instructor is good at pulling needles out of haystacks. His lectures regarding the papers we read helped me massively.

His strongest feature was his ability to express an idea in his mind without hesitation while speaking.

Yet he had peculiar and idiosyncratic views on how philosophy should be done, but expected them to be universally accepted. His weakest trait was his unwavering confidence that only his own opinion was correct on each and every possible subject, and his dismissive (rather than engaging) attitude whenever anyone expressed a dissident opinion. His aim seemed to be to impose his own ideas on us students rather than to actually teach us something, and his indifference to our learning was such that he could launch into tirades without seeing the slightest sign that others were following the subject.

He was punctual during the semester, that is a good point. However, I had the feeling that "if I say something that he does not agree with, he will not listen to my question or ideas" very often. That made me not wanting speaking during the class. He usually interrupts when someone asks a question. The class is designed as if we are only interested in his questions and ideas. It was not a welcomed discussion place that I feel free to talk. Also, he was rude when he was giving feedbacks. I still have to write my final paper and I will not write my own ideas in that but I will write what professor Fatollahi thinks right so that I can have a good grade.

In the first half of the semester, I was able to understand because there were more historical topics, but in the second half, everything was very difficult for me. The statistical and mathematical concepts in the course content were sometimes explained as if we all knew them, which made it very difficult for me to understand most of the things. I did not find it meaningful to use so much statistics and mathematics in a philosophy course. If what was to be explained could be explained verbally, why were concepts used that most people in the course did not know? If this was necessary, the course could have been designed in such a way that these concepts were explained one by one. Although it was obvious that the instructor was quite knowledgeable about the subject, I do not think he was able to convey what he knew to me. Also, I would like to mention the instructor's attitude towards those who spoke during the course. Even if someone made a very clear and understandable point and developed a counter-argument, the instructor's first reactions resulted in not fully understanding the explained point, and sometimes even interrupting the student and directly rejecting it. This situation was a point that tired me a lot throughout the semester. To give an example, even if there was more than one interpretation of a reading in the literature, the result was that if something was said against the interpretation accepted by the teacher, it was directly rejected. Finally, I did not find the feedback he gave to our writings pedagogically constructive at all. His discouraging and sometimes disrespectful criticism of what we wrote without fully understanding it completely destroyed the little motivation I had for the course.

The general problem with the instructor is that he assumed that we knew advanced logic and statistics. One did not have to know those to get an ok grade, yet most of the classes after the second half of the classes were filled with advanced logic and statistics, so most of the time, I think many of us had very little idea what was going on, and I think he was aware of it.
course:

The name of the course is very misleading and there were no syllabus when we were choosing the courses that we are gonna take. It is not the history of analytic philosophy, but it is "of science" as the professor stated on the first lecture. However, analytic philosophy does not start with Aristotales or it does not capture Newton. The course is very misleading. However, I liked to see the application of statistical methods.

Great course overall. As someone who does not deal with math regularly, the math stuff was quite challenging to grasp in 1-2 weeks. As a solution maybe optional math practice assignments could be given at the start of the semester.
Also, sometimes the in-class discussions got a bit abstract, so it got difficult to contribute. To address this issue, more emphasis could be made on some actual empirical work relevant to a given topic.

Before this course, I didn't have a special interest in philosophy of science, but I had at least a belief that there might be issues that would interest me on this subject. This course shattered even this tiny motivation and made me never want to mention the name of philosophy of science ever again.
I don't think it's a good philosophy course overall unless it covers statistics and math concepts one by one, which are present in most of the readings in the second half of the semester.
